text: It is a matter of opinion. The fact is that it is not a question of machines, but a question of machines and men together. When the machines are of a certain character, the men are not weakened by relying on them, and when the machines are of a different character, the men are weakened by relying on them. To understand which, we must understand the character of the machines. There are machines which do not weaken men but strengthen them, and there are machines which do not strengthen men but weaken them. The weakening of men through machinery is a consequence of the nature of the machinery. It is not a question of machines, but a question of machines and men together. In this way, in the case of the machines we have mentioned before, which are machines made by men and not by themselves, the machines do not weaken men. In the case of the machines made by themselves, the machines do weaken men.

It depends on the mechanical means employed. It can be used so as to help the mind, or as a substitute for the mind. Of course, the mind cannot profit by a machine that is no more than a machine. A person who is a mere machine is a machine. But a person who uses the machine intelligently, as a means of training the mind, may find that the machine has helped him. It may be used to help the mind, but it must never be used as a substitute for the mind. A machine cannot think. We may use a machine to make us think. But we must not think that a machine can do our thinking. If we are to have a machine, it must be a means to an end, not an end in itself. That is, our aim should not be to make machines of ourselves, but to make machines help us to be men. The mere fact that a machine is a machine does not prevent its being used intelligently. The former is right. Machines do not weaken men's capacities. Machines make men; machines are not made by men; machines are not the outcome of human ingenuity; machines are not the result of human invention. Machines are the creation of God. Man's function is to control, to guide, to regulate. Human capacities are strengthened by the use of machines.

The truth lies between the two. If you rely on machines to do all the work, you can relax and let your mind drift. But this is not necessary. If you have a mind of your own, you can make the machine your servant, and use your mind to control it. And even when you are using the machine, you can keep your mind on the work you are doing. This is a matter of training. A trained mind can work to advantage with a machine.

In a general way, it may be said that the more automatic the machine is, the less it is likely to weaken the human brain. The simplest machines, such as typewriters, are not likely to weaken the brain. They are, in fact, great time savers and time savers are brain builders. The more automatic a machine is, the more it is likely to weaken the human brain; but the extent to which this is true depends on the particular machine. A machine which is used to do the same thing over and over again, as in making pins, does not weaken the brain so much as a machine which requires that the brain be called upon for a variety of work. This is because the same thing has to be done over and over again and the mind has become accustomed to doing it.

We may hold that the develop ment of machines does not weaken human capacities, although they may never appear so prominently. Machines have been responsible for the present-day overcrowding and high rents, and have made the lives of those who have to live in them on a low standard of existence. The same criticism applies to the rapid growth of factories; but the first effect of factories on wages is to increase them. In the long run, however, factories have a degrading effect on the worker, because they are built in such a way that they are unhealthy places to live in. In a factory the worker is restricted in his movements and is dependent on mechanical power, and his work is often monotonous and mechanical. No wonder, then, that the factory workers are deteriorating physically and mentally. Machine-made goods have also a deteriorating effect on the worker; they are made on a low standard of living, and take the place of home-made goods which are made under better conditions. The result is that there are more people working at low rates, and the value of their services is thus reduced.

On the one hand, by relying on machines we have not to rely on our own minds, but can rely on the minds of others; and on the other hand, by relying on machines we have not to rely on our own bodies, but can rely on the bodies of others. Thus, in both cases, we rely on the minds and bodies of others. In saying that we rely on the minds of others, I mean that we rely on the steam-engine. In saying that we rely on the bodies of others, I mean that we rely on the operators. The man who relies on machines is not weak, but strong.
It does, because machines can do work that men can do, and thereby does away with the necessity for muscular effort, and hence renders the muscles less capable of effort.

There is no doubt that relying on machines weakens the human faculties. Blind reliance on a machine is a species of superstition, and the more of such superstitions that are held the weaker the human faculties will become. But the right use of machines will strengthen the human faculties, because it will enable a man to dispense with those intellectual operations which are the most difficult to perform. For instance, by the use of the slide rule, which is a machine for performing calculations, anyone can perform arithmetical operations with ease and rapidity, which without the aid of the slide rule would be difficult and laborious.

We cannot say that it does not weaken human capacities. It is, for example, the displacement of the woodchopper by the power-boring machine that causes unemployment and misery. On the other hand, the use of machines is not without its benefits. The great increase in wealth, which has allowed a great development of culture, is due to the machine. Furthermore, the more man invents machines, the more his capacities will develop. In a sense, the machine is a means of liberating the capacities of man. The machine-mind is a product of the machine. The machine is a liberator. The machine is a liberator in the same way that the factory is a liberator. Both have liberated the human being from the slavery of manual labor. The machine-mind, as well as the factory-mind, is a machine-mind. The factory-mind is a machine-mind in the sense that it uses machines. The former are right. For instance, in the past, people of all nations used to rely on machines only when they were forced to do so. For example, the English used to rely on machines to perform their work only when they were not able to perform it by human labour. The result was that the English were not as efficient as they are now. Even at the present time, those who rely on machines are not as efficient as those who rely on their own labour. In the future, those who rely on machines will be in a worse position. At the present time machines are not used as much as they ought to be. On the contrary, they are used far too much. The result is that people are not as healthy as they ought to be. If people were to rely not only on machines but also on their own labour, then they would be more healthy than they are now.

It is not possible to prove what is right or wrong in these matters. Machine production, like all the other means of production, is in the process of being modified. The Chinese had a remarkable system of irrigation, which Europe adopted without much change, but felt later that it was not up to date. We have begun to do the same thing with machines. It is not yet clear how we shall proceed.
That is a question which is never likely to be settled. It depends on the individual, and on the whole, a machine is more likely to strengthen a feeble man than to weaken a strong one.

In abstracto, if we consider human nature to be constant, it is right to say that machines do not necessarily weaken human capacities. On the other hand, if we consider human nature, and especially the human mind, to be variable, we must say that machines do weaken human capacities. The difference between the two views is only a difference in the way we think of human nature; the difference is not an absolute difference. That which seems to be a universal truth, when we think of human nature in the abstract, becomes a particular truth, when we think of human nature in the concrete. From the last point of view we may say that machines do weaken human capacities. The question, therefore, is not one which can be answered by any set formula, but one which has to be answered by taking into account all the circumstances of the individual case.

Both are right. Machines do not weaken human capacities; rather, they multiply them. Machines do not weaken human capacities, for they do not do any work for which human muscles are equipped. Machines do not weaken human capacities; they do not undertake any activity for which human faculties are not equipped. Machines do not weaken human capacities; they do not perform any actions that are not within the compass of human faculties.

This depends on what we mean by human capacities. If we mean capacity to make machines, then it is true that mechanical invention tends to diminish the supply of such capacity. If we mean power to use machines, it may be that there is no such diminution. Certain it is that capacity for using machines is extensively cultivated, and that the supply of such capacity is steadily growing. This is shown, for example, in the spread in recent years of mechanical devices for housework, or in the spread of scientific management, where the introduction of motion study and the use of mechanical devices has increased enormously the output of men and women without overtaxing their physical strength. The same is true of the use of machinery in agriculture and in the industries. It is true of the use of machinery for transportation and communication. There is no doubt that the use of machinery, properly handled, is compatible with full human development for the worker.
The dependence on machines is good for us; the abuse of them is bad. We cannot do without them, but we must not become their slaves.

In the first place, machines are only used when human capacities are weak. If human capacities were strong, machines would have no scope. It is not human capacities that are weak, but machines that are strong. Therefore, without using machines, human capacities cannot be strong. The first opinion is the correct one. Man is the only animal that can work with tools. His hands are the only ones that can work. The more he uses his hands, the more he develops them. If, on the contrary, he relies on machines, he is not obliged to develop his hands; his hands are his tools; he is a machine himself. The less he works with his hands, the more they are weakened.

To trust to a machine is a practice which, if kept up, tends to weaken the human capacities. It is a practice which, if followed up for a number of generations, tends to weaken the human capacities. But it is a practice which, if followed up for a few generations, tends to strengthen the human capacities. The first generation will learn to work the machine; they will do a great deal of work; they will grow into a race of very hardy workers. Their offspring will do a great deal of work, but will not do it quite as well; they will grow into a race of somewhat less hardy workers, but of somewhat greater dexterity. Their offspring will do a little less work, but will do it with greater dexterity; they will grow into a race of somewhat less hardy workers, but of somewhat greater dexterity. The descendants of the descendants will do a little less work, but will do it with greater dexterity; they will grow into a race of somewhat less hardy workers, but of somewhat greater dexterity. Especially in the case of machines for performing mechanical operations, such as the typewriter and the adding machine, the human capacity to learn is called out in a way that would not be required if the machine were not there. The mastery of the machine also is an admirable training in observation and accuracy, and the human touch is not altogether eliminated by the machine. In the case of such machines as the piano, where the touch is a vital part of the performance, the machine does not train the capacity of the performer as much as the study of the piano.

The truth probably lies between the two views. No doubt it is true that the machine, by its unceasing demands on the mind and body of the worker, tends to make him incapable of any strenuous effort of his own. But the machine, on the other hand, by relieving the worker of the necessity of satisfying his wants directly by his own efforts, would seem to give him the opportunity of devoting himself to higher things, if only he values such things as highly as the necessary effort would imply. Here, as elsewhere, the question of value is the crucial one. For the man who values his own comforts above every other consideration, the machine is a curse. For the man who values his own self-development above every other consideration, the machine may be a blessing. The ultimate test is the state of mind of the worker.

Though mechanism may serve us, it cannot be our master. The machine is the slave of man, but the man must remain the master. If it is not so, man is degraded and degraded not only physically but morally and intellectually. It is much better to have a man who is a good mechanic, than a machine that is a good man. Machinery can never be a substitute for man. It has never been a substitute for man, even in a factory, where it is said to have been most successful.

The first statement is correct; the second is correct. Reliance on machines weakens human capacities in the same proportion as the machine eliminates the necessity of the human to exert his capacities, or in proportion to the number of machines he uses. Reliance on machines weakens human capacities in proportion as the machine is a substitute for the human. Reliance on machines strengthens human capacities in proportion as the machine is a complement of human capacities, or in proportion to the number of machines used by the human. It is, of course, true that in proportion as the machine is a substitute for the human, it weakens human capacities. This is one of the main reasons why the machines are hated, and why the human is at war with the machine. But it is also true that in proportion as the machine is a complement of the human, it strengthens human capacities. This is one of the reasons why the machine is loved and why the human is at peace with the machine.

The machine is an instrument which contains within itself a force. This force can be applied and used by man, but he himself need not be present. It is quite natural that the machine should weaken the capacities of man, because it frees him from the necessity of using his capacity.

The first is right, for the same reason that walking on crutches does not weaken the legs. The legs are better off for having the crutches to lean on, and the brain is better off for having the machine to help it.
The question of whether it is right to use machines depends on whether the use of them weakens human capacities. If the use of machines weakens human capacities, it is wrong to use them.

Both are right. If we rely on machines to do the work which our own intelligences can do better, we are doing ourselves an injustice and are crippling our powers. But when we call upon machines to do work which we cannot do without them, we are acting wisely. The use of machines is thus seen to be a matter of intelligence rather than of weakness.

Let us see what this argument of the Socialists amounts to. They say, "We shall get rid of individual workers, and thus have more people who can enjoy themselves." This is a very common argument used by the Socialists. But I must say that I have heard a good many men who have worked hard all their lives and who have never had any chance of enjoying themselves, and who have been obliged to work all day long for their bread. How could they enjoy being Socialists? As a rule, they are the most miserable men I have ever met.

Weakening of capacities is a matter of degree. The question whether human capacities are weakened by relying on machines depends on the degree of reliance. If the degree of reliance is small, there is no weakening. It is only in the degree of reliance that there is weakness.

The question, in the form in which it is put, is ambiguous. If it is meant that the use of machines does not weaken the man who uses them, it is doubtless true that it does not. If it is meant that the invention of machines which are not used by the masses does not weaken the race, the answer is, yes, it does. The machine does not weaken the man who uses it, but it weakens immensely the race of men that does not use it.

The human understanding and the human memory are not weakened by the use of machines, but it is only the memory of things which have been previously learned that is weakened. If machines were the only means of learning the things which the memory retains and which are taken into the mind by the senses, then the mind would be weakened. The mind would no longer have an opportunity to make a selection of things to be remembered. But the use of machines is not necessary for that purpose, except during the first period of learning. As soon as the machine method begins to be understood, the mind begins to select the things which are to be remembered. We are all agreed that in the past the human being has been weakened through relying on machines, because the machines have been too complicated for him to manage; but in the future, though he will still be dehumanized, he will be dehumanized in a different way. The machines will be less complicated, and he will be able to manage them easily; but he will not be able to manage them by himself. It will always be necessary to have a manager, who will be paid for doing it. This manager will be a skilled workman, but not necessarily a human being. He will be a human being, but not a conscious human being, and he will have to be trained in a special way for his job. He will have to be trained in a special way, because he will have to be trained to the human standard of behaviour, and to the human standard of human virtues. The first opinion is right if we consider human capacities in the light of their independent activity. The second opinion is right if we consider them in the light of their relation to the machines. While machines are increasing and men are becoming the slaves of machines, their capacities are weakened, and they are growing stupid. But if the machines are being brought under human control their capacities are being strengthened.

The machine does not weaken the capacities of the human body, but it weakens the capacity of the human mind. The machine does not weaken the capacity of the human body, because the muscles of the human body do not need human intelligence. The brain has no geometrical sense and no mechanical perception; and machines, as a rule, do not need a geometrical sense and a mechanical perception. Machines, as an example, do not need to know that a ball, dropped from the hand, will fall to the ground. To drop a ball from the hand requires no geometrical sense and no mechanical perception. This is why the machine does not weaken the muscles of the human body. But machines, as a rule, do need a human intelligence, as for instance, if the machine is to be used for the production of a new machine, or for some other purpose. Thus the machine does weaken the capacity of the human mind.

Relying on machines may or may not weaken human capacities. If machines are used to do what is essentially the work of the human being, and if the machines are used for mechanical purposes only, they will not weaken human capacities. If machines are used to do things which are essentially the work of the human being, and if the machines are used for humanitarian purposes only, they will not weaken human capacities. But if machines are used for mechanical purposes without humanitarian purposes, they will weaken human capacities. If machines are used for humanitarian purposes without mechanical purposes, they will not weaken human capacities.
